title: Waterboy vs Liquid IV: Which Is Better for Hydration and Hangovers?
excerpt: Waterboy vs Liquid IV: how their sodium, sugar, and potassium compare, what Waterboy Weekend Recovery adds, which costs what, and which to pick for a hangover or daily use.
metaDescription: Waterboy vs Liquid IV compared: sodium, sugar, potassium, and price, plus which is better for a hangover, workouts, keto, and everyday hydration.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Waterboy and Liquid I.V. are both electrolyte stick packs you stir into water, but they're built on different ideas. Liquid I.V.'s original formula is close to a classic oral rehydration drink: a moderate amount of sodium, a fair amount of potassium, and about 11 grams of sugar that helps your gut pull water in. Waterboy is sugar-free across its lineup, sweetened with stevia, and sells separate formulas for everyday use, workouts, and "weekend recovery." If you want the most textbook rehydration drink for a hangover or a queasy, dehydrated day, Liquid I.V. original is the more proven design. If you avoid sugar, eat low-carb, or plan to drink electrolytes most days, Waterboy Daily Hydration is the lighter, sugar-free pick. Neither one cures or prevents a hangover. They help with the dehydration part, and that's all.

**The quick picks:**

- **Hangover with nausea, or you haven't eaten yet:** Liquid I.V. original, one stick in 16 ounces of water. The small dose of sugar helps absorption and gives you a little fuel.
- **Everyday hydration with no sugar:** Waterboy Daily Hydration, or Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free if you want the Liquid I.V. flavor range.
- **Long, sweaty workouts or hot days:** Waterboy Workout Hydration, which carries roughly twice the sodium of Liquid I.V.
- **Keto, low-carb, or watching blood sugar:** Waterboy (any line) or Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free.
- **High blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or you take water pills:** talk to your doctor before using either one regularly.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article compares general label information and research. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor before using electrolyte mixes regularly if** you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or diabetes, or you take blood pressure medicines, diuretics (water pills), or potassium-sparing drugs. **Get medical help right away if** you can't keep fluids down for several hours, you're vomiting repeatedly, you've barely urinated all day, you feel faint or confused, or someone who has been drinking is hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, or having a seizure. Those are signs of serious dehydration or alcohol poisoning, and a drink mix is not the answer. Call 911 in an emergency.

## Waterboy vs Liquid I.V. at a Glance

Here's how the main versions compare per stick. These are approximate figures from the brands' published labels and retail listings at the time of writing. Both companies reformulate from time to time, so check the box in front of you for exact numbers.

| | Waterboy Daily Hydration | Waterboy Workout Hydration | Waterboy Weekend Recovery | Liquid I.V. Hydration Multiplier (original) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sodium | ~550 mg | ~1,000 mg | ~1,100 mg | ~500 mg |
| Potassium | ~140 mg | ~400 mg | ~350 mg | ~370 mg |
| Magnesium | ~20 mg | ~50 mg | ~50 mg | Not a significant source |
| Sugar | 0 g | 0 g | 0 g | ~11 g (cane sugar and dextrose) |
| Calories | 0 | ~10 | ~5 | ~45 |
| Sweetener | Organic stevia | Organic stevia | Organic stevia | Sugar (Sugar-Free line uses allulose and other sweeteners) |
| Extras | None to speak of | Vitamin C, B12, L-glutamine | Ginger, L-theanine, vitamin C, B12 | Vitamin C and several B vitamins |
| Typical price per stick | Roughly $1.10 | Roughly $1.40 | Roughly $1.65 | Roughly $1 to $1.60 depending on pack size |

The headline difference is simple. **Liquid I.V. pairs moderate sodium with sugar, the way medical rehydration drinks do. Waterboy skips the sugar entirely and lets you choose how much sodium you want by picking a formula.** Most "which is better" questions come down to whether you want the sugar and how salty you want your drink.

## The Core Difference: Sugar or No Sugar

This is the part most comparison articles skip, and it's the one that matters most for rehydration.

### Why Liquid I.V. includes sugar

Your small intestine has a transporter that moves sodium and glucose into the body together, and water follows them. This is the basis of oral rehydration solutions (ORS), the simple salt-and-sugar drinks the World Health Organization recommends for dehydration from diarrhea. Their adoption is widely credited with saving millions of lives, which is about as strong a track record as any nutrition idea gets.

Liquid I.V. markets this as "Cellular Transport Technology." That's a brand name for the same well-known sodium-plus-glucose principle, not a new discovery. Its roughly 11 grams of sugar per stick is about a quarter of a can of regular soda. For one stick on a rough morning, that's a modest amount, and it does real work in helping fluid absorb.

### Why Waterboy leaves it out

Waterboy is aimed at people who want electrolytes without sugar or calories: people on keto or low-carb diets, people managing blood sugar, and people who want to drink electrolytes every day without adding sugar to their diet. It's sweetened with a small amount of organic stevia, and it uses pink Himalayan salt, potassium citrate, and magnesium as the mineral sources.

Without glucose, you lose the sodium-glucose co-transport boost. That doesn't make sugar-free electrolytes useless. Your body still absorbs water and sodium without sugar, especially if you're eating food alongside your drink, and most people who are mildly dehydrated rehydrate fine with water, salt, and a meal. It just means Waterboy is not an oral rehydration solution in the medical sense, and it isn't designed to be.

### What this means in practice

- **If you're also eating,** the sugar question matters much less. Food supplies carbohydrate and salt, and your gut will handle the rest. Waterboy plus breakfast is a perfectly reasonable hangover morning.
- **If you can't face food yet,** the sugar in Liquid I.V. is doing you a favor. It helps absorption and gives you a little energy when your blood sugar may be on the low side after drinking.
- **If you're drinking electrolytes daily,** the sugar adds up. Two or three Liquid I.V. sticks a day is 22 to 33 grams of added sugar. Waterboy avoids that entirely.

## Sodium: How Salty Is Each One?

Sodium is the electrolyte you lose most in sweat, and it's the one that most helps your body hold on to water. It's more useful to think about how concentrated the drink is than the number on the stick, because you decide how much water to use.

Here's roughly what each looks like mixed in 16 ounces (about half a liter) of water:

- **Liquid I.V. original:** about 500 mg of sodium, which works out to roughly 45 millimoles per liter. That's a little under the WHO's reduced-osmolarity ORS, which sits at 75 millimoles per liter. In plain terms, it's moderately salty.
- **Waterboy Daily Hydration:** about 550 mg, roughly 50 millimoles per liter. Very close to Liquid I.V. on salt.
- **Waterboy Workout Hydration:** about 1,000 mg, roughly 90 millimoles per liter if you use 16 ounces. That's saltier than medical ORS. Many people will prefer it in 24 to 32 ounces.
- **Waterboy Weekend Recovery:** about 1,100 mg, in the same range as the Workout formula.

So the sodium story is more nuanced than "Waterboy is saltier." **Waterboy Daily and Liquid I.V. original carry about the same sodium.** Only Waterboy's Workout and Weekend Recovery lines are roughly double.

For context, US dietary guidelines suggest keeping sodium under about 2,300 mg a day. One Waterboy Weekend Recovery stick is close to half of that. That's fine for someone who sweated through a long run or a hot day. It's a lot to add on top of a typical salty diet if you're just sitting at a desk, and it's worth a conversation with your doctor if your blood pressure runs high.

## Potassium and Magnesium

**Potassium** is the other big electrolyte. It works with sodium to manage fluid balance inside and outside your cells, and alcohol can push it down, especially if you vomit or have diarrhea.

- Liquid I.V. original has about 370 mg per stick, a good share for a drink mix.
- Waterboy Daily Hydration has only about 140 mg. Its sodium-to-potassium ratio is close to 4 to 1, which some reviewers have pointed out leans heavily toward sodium.
- Waterboy Workout (about 400 mg) and Weekend Recovery (about 350 mg) are in the same range as Liquid I.V.

None of these comes close to meeting your daily potassium needs, which sit in the thousands of milligrams. Food does that job far better. A banana, a potato, a bowl of yogurt, or a glass of orange juice each adds a meaningful amount. If you're relying on a drink mix for potassium, eat something too.

**Magnesium** is where Waterboy has a small edge. All its lines include some, from about 20 mg in Daily to about 50 mg in Workout and Recovery. Liquid I.V.'s original formula isn't a meaningful magnesium source. That said, 50 mg is a small slice of the daily requirement of roughly 310 to 420 mg for adults, so neither drink is a real magnesium supplement. Our guide to [magnesium and alcohol](/never-hungover/magnesium-and-alcohol) covers whether it's worth adding separately.

## Waterboy Weekend Recovery vs Liquid I.V. for a Hangover

This is the head-to-head most people searching this topic actually care about, because Waterboy sells a formula aimed squarely at the morning after.

**What Weekend Recovery adds:** on top of a high-sodium electrolyte base, it includes ginger extract, L-theanine, vitamin C, and vitamin B12, all with no sugar.

Here's an honest look at those extras:

- **Ginger** has reasonable evidence for easing nausea in general, mostly from studies on pregnancy-related nausea and nausea after surgery or chemotherapy. There's no good evidence that it helps a hangover specifically, but if your stomach is unsettled, it's a sensible ingredient. The dose in a drink mix is usually well below what's used in nausea studies, so don't expect too much.
- **L-theanine** is an amino acid from tea that some people find calming. There's no good evidence it improves hangover symptoms.
- **Vitamin C and B12** are common in hangover products. Drinking can affect how your body handles some B vitamins, but a single dose the morning after hasn't been shown to change how you feel.

**What Liquid I.V. original offers:** moderate sodium, solid potassium, sugar for absorption and energy, and a handful of vitamins. It's less salty than Weekend Recovery, which a queasy stomach often tolerates better.

**Which one to pick for a hangover:**

- **If you're nauseous and not eating yet,** Liquid I.V. original is the better fit. Less salt, plus sugar for absorption and fuel.
- **If you're eating, avoiding sugar, or sweated a lot the night before** (dancing, a hot venue, a summer outdoor event), Waterboy Weekend Recovery is reasonable. Mix it in more water than you think, at least 16 ounces and possibly more, and sip it rather than gulping.
- **If you're vomiting and can't keep things down,** neither is the right tool. Small sips of a true oral rehydration solution such as Pedialyte are a better match, and if you can't keep even that down for several hours, get medical care.

For a wider view of the category, our [comparison of electrolyte drinks for hangovers](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) ranks the main options side by side, and our deeper look at [Liquid I.V. for a hangover](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-for-hangover) covers when it helps and when it doesn't. For the bigger picture on why drinking drains electrolytes in the first place, see our guide to [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol).

## What Electrolytes Can and Can't Do for a Hangover

It's worth being clear about this, because both brands lean on recovery language in their marketing.

**What they can do.** Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, a hormone that normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. That's why you urinate more when you drink. If you also sweat, vomit, or simply don't drink much water, you can wake up somewhat dehydrated. An electrolyte drink can help you replace fluid and sodium a bit faster than plain water, especially if you aren't eating yet. That can ease thirst, dry mouth, lightheadedness, and some of the headache. Our guide on [whether alcohol really dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) explains how much of this is real.

**What they can't do.** Research on hangovers has found that dehydration is only part of the picture. Hangover severity doesn't track neatly with dehydration markers in the blood. Other drivers include inflammation, poor sleep, acetaldehyde (a toxic by-product of alcohol breakdown), and congeners in darker drinks. No electrolyte drink addresses those. There is no good evidence that Waterboy, Liquid I.V., or any other electrolyte mix prevents a hangover.

**The practical takeaway:** use an electrolyte drink as one part of your recovery, alongside water, food, sleep, and time. Don't expect it to undo a heavy night. For the habits with the best evidence, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## When to Drink Them: Before Bed or the Morning After?

Both work in either slot. A few practical tips:

- **Before bed:** one stick with a full glass of water can start rehydrating you while you sleep. The downside is a likely bathroom trip at 4 a.m. If your stomach is unsettled, Waterboy Daily or Liquid I.V. original are gentler than the high-sodium Waterboy lines.
- **The morning after:** this is the more common choice and often the more useful one, because you can pair it with food. One stick, then plain water through the day.
- **During the night out:** alternating alcoholic drinks with water does more good than any drink mix. Our guide to [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers timing in more detail.

Two sticks in 24 hours is plenty for most healthy adults. More than that, especially of the high-sodium Waterboy lines, pushes sodium intake up quickly without much extra benefit.

## Taste, Mixing, and Convenience

**Taste.** This is personal, but there are patterns. Liquid I.V. tastes sweet and fruity in a way that's familiar from sports drinks, because it contains real sugar. Waterboy tastes lighter and less sweet, with the slightly different finish stevia gives. People who dislike stevia tend not to like Waterboy. People who find Liquid I.V. too sugary tend to prefer it. The higher-sodium Waterboy lines can taste noticeably salty in only 16 ounces.

**Mixing.** Both dissolve easily in cold water with a stir or a shake. Waterboy's Daily stick is small (about 3 grams), so it mixes very quickly. Liquid I.V. sticks are larger because of the sugar.

**Availability.** Liquid I.V. is everywhere: big-box stores, grocery chains, pharmacies, warehouse clubs, and convenience stores. Waterboy has spread into more retailers, including some major grocery chains, but it's still easier to find online or direct from the brand. If you want something you can grab at any store on a Sunday morning, Liquid I.V. wins.

**Variety.** Liquid I.V. has a large flavor range plus Sugar-Free, Energy, Sleep, and Immune Support lines. Waterboy has a smaller set of flavors but splits its products by purpose (Daily, Workout, Weekend Recovery), which makes it easier to pick a sodium level.

## Price: Which Is Cheaper?

They're in a similar range, and prices move a lot with sales, subscriptions, and pack sizes. Rough figures at the time of writing:

- **Waterboy Daily Hydration:** around $1.10 a stick, with a discount for subscriptions.
- **Waterboy Workout Hydration:** around $1.40 a stick.
- **Waterboy Weekend Recovery:** around $1.65 a stick.
- **Liquid I.V. original:** roughly $1 to $1.60 a stick, often less in big warehouse-club packs.

For pure value, store-brand oral rehydration packets and powders are usually cheaper than either. And for many mild cases, a glass of water, a pinch of salt in your food, and a banana do most of the job for a few cents. If you'd like to make your own, our [homemade electrolyte drink recipe](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink) shows how.

## Pros and Cons

### Waterboy

**Pros**

- Zero sugar and close to zero calories across every line
- Separate formulas let you choose your sodium level
- Daily Hydration is gentle on sodium for everyday use
- Includes some magnesium
- Short, simple ingredient list

**Cons**

- Not a true oral rehydration solution, since there's no glucose to speed absorption
- Daily Hydration is low in potassium
- Workout and Weekend Recovery are high in sodium for casual use
- Weekend Recovery's extras (ginger, L-theanine, vitamins) have no good evidence of easing hangovers at these doses
- Harder to find in stores than Liquid I.V.
- Stevia aftertaste bothers some people

### Liquid I.V.

**Pros**

- Built on the well-established salt-plus-sugar rehydration principle
- Good potassium for a drink mix
- Moderate sodium that most people tolerate well
- Sold almost everywhere
- Large flavor and product range, including a Sugar-Free line

**Cons**

- About 11 grams of sugar per stick, which adds up with daily use
- Not ideal for strict keto or for people managing blood sugar (the Sugar-Free version helps)
- Very little magnesium in the original formula
- "Cellular Transport Technology" is marketing language for a basic, long-known principle
- Lower sodium than you may want after very heavy sweating

## Who Should Be Careful With Either One

Electrolyte drinks are safe for most healthy adults in normal amounts, but they aren't for everyone. Check with a doctor before using them regularly if you:

- **Have high blood pressure.** Extra sodium can push it up, and the high-sodium Waterboy lines add a lot.
- **Have kidney disease.** Your kidneys may not clear extra sodium or potassium normally.
- **Have heart failure.** Extra sodium can lead to fluid buildup.
- **Take blood pressure medicines, diuretics, or potassium-sparing drugs.** Some of these change how your body handles sodium and potassium, so the extra from a drink mix can matter.
- **Have diabetes.** Liquid I.V.'s sugar counts toward your carbohydrates. Waterboy or Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free avoid that, but you should still ask your care team.

And to repeat the important part: if you can't keep fluids down, haven't urinated in many hours, feel faint or confused, or someone who's been drinking is hard to wake or breathing oddly, get medical help. That isn't a hangover anymore, and a stick pack is not the fix.

## Where DHM Fits In

Electrolytes deal with fluid and minerals. They do nothing for how your body breaks down alcohol, which is where some people look at supplements.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. It's promising, not proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in people. It also doesn't replace water, food, sleep, or drinking less.

If you want to try it alongside your usual hydration routine, some people use [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) or the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take medication, read our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) first.

## The Bottom Line

- **Liquid I.V. original** is the better fit for a hangover morning when you're queasy or haven't eaten, because its sugar helps fluid absorption and it's moderately salty.
- **Waterboy Daily Hydration** is the better fit for sugar-free, everyday use. On sodium it's nearly identical to Liquid I.V., but it's lower in potassium.
- **Waterboy Workout and Weekend Recovery** carry about twice the sodium. They suit heavy sweaters and hot days more than desk days.
- Weekend Recovery's ginger may help a little with nausea, but there's no good evidence its extras ease hangovers.
- Neither brand prevents or cures a hangover. Water, food, sleep, and drinking less still do most of the work.
- If you have high blood pressure, kidney or heart problems, or take water pills, ask your doctor before using either one regularly.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Waterboy or Liquid I.V. better?**

It depends on what you need. Liquid I.V. original pairs moderate sodium with about 11 grams of sugar, the same salt-plus-sugar idea behind medical rehydration drinks, which makes it a good fit for hangovers and general rehydration. Waterboy is sugar-free and sold in separate formulas, so it suits people avoiding sugar, people on keto, and people who drink electrolytes every day. Neither is better across the board.

**Is Waterboy or Liquid I.V. better for a hangover?**

For most people with nausea who haven't eaten yet, Liquid I.V. original is the easier choice, because its sugar helps fluid absorption and it's less salty than Waterboy's recovery formula. Waterboy Weekend Recovery is reasonable if you're eating, avoiding sugar, or sweated a lot the night before. Mix it in plenty of water and sip it. Neither one prevents or cures a hangover; they only help with the dehydration part.

**Does Waterboy have more sodium than Liquid I.V.?**

It depends on the line. Waterboy Daily Hydration has about 550 mg of sodium per stick, almost the same as Liquid I.V. original's roughly 500 mg. Waterboy Workout Hydration and Weekend Recovery have roughly 1,000 to 1,100 mg, about twice as much. Check the label, since both brands update their formulas.

**Does Waterboy have sugar?**

No. Waterboy's lines list 0 grams of sugar and are sweetened with organic stevia. Liquid I.V.'s original formula has about 11 grams of sugar per stick, and its Sugar-Free line uses other sweeteners instead.

**Does Waterboy Weekend Recovery actually work for hangovers?**

It can help with the dehydration part of a hangover, like any electrolyte drink. Its ginger has some general evidence for easing nausea, though the dose in a drink mix is usually lower than in studies. There's no good evidence that its L-theanine or vitamins improve hangover symptoms. It won't address poor sleep, inflammation, or the other drivers of a hangover.

**Can you drink Waterboy or Liquid I.V. every day?**

Healthy adults can, but most people don't need to. Waterboy Daily Hydration is the gentler daily option because it has no sugar and moderate sodium. Liquid I.V.'s sugar adds up across several sticks a day, and Waterboy's high-sodium lines push sodium intake up quickly. If you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, or heart failure, or take blood pressure medicines or water pills, check with a doctor before making either a daily habit.

**Which is cheaper, Waterboy or Liquid I.V.?**

They're in a similar range. Waterboy Daily Hydration runs around $1.10 a stick, with the Workout and Weekend Recovery lines higher, around $1.40 to $1.65. Liquid I.V. is roughly $1 to $1.60 a stick depending on pack size, often less at warehouse clubs. Prices change with sales and subscriptions, and store-brand rehydration packets are usually cheaper than both.

**Is Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free the same as Waterboy?**

Not quite. Both skip sugar, but they use different sweeteners and mineral amounts. Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free uses allulose and other sweeteners, while Waterboy uses stevia. If you want a sugar-free drink, compare the labels for sodium and potassium and pick the one whose taste you prefer.
